column2: Neither man took a chair when they left the house. Ji lived near Qingbo Gate, not far from the Willows Where Orioles Sing, so they walked there at leisure and sat down in a restaurant called Bieyoutian, “Another World.” Hu calmly discussed the choice of dishes and wine with Ji, as though they were old friends accustomed to meeting over a cup. “Brother Xueyan,” Ji asked directly, “does Prefect Wang really believe that no one but me can handle the Xincheng case?” “I'm not quite sure. But the day before yesterday I heard him complaining about Governor Huang.” Hu sipped his wine and continued casually. “He said the authorities had sent so many commissioners, yet few were of any use. Better to have sent Ji alone; then there would have been nothing to say.” “What did he mean, ‘nothing to say’?” “From his tone, I think he meant that you would have had no grounds to refuse. If you were the only commissioner and he needed your help, I imagine you could hardly decline. But with so many here, it seems awkward for him to insist on choosing you.” “Yes,” Ji said. “I understand his difficulty.”

And what would he do about it? Hu asked himself. But he did not want to press too hard or too soon. In fact, he felt no urgency, for he had almost completely understood Ji's temperament. Once persuaded, Ji would be more eager to help than anyone. Sure enough, he continued, “This is a duty I should not shrink from. But Prefect Wang must be willing to listen to me.” Hu knew how to play his part. “What exactly is involved? I still don't fully understand. It's official business, so I'd better say little. Brother Heling, you've doubtless heard that Prefect Wang and I are unusually close. Though you and I have only just met, we've taken to each other immediately. Frankly, I aspire to a friendship above my station. If you're willing to accept me, I'm sure we shall become the best of friends. For that reason...” He paused, assuming a resolute expression. “I must consider your interests too. Friendship cannot mean helping one man at another's expense. Wouldn't you agree?” “Indeed.” Ji nodded deeply. “Brother Xueyan, this is no empty compliment: it's rare to find a merchant with the qualities of the persuasive strategists of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.” Hu did not understand the reference, but knew it was praise. Modesty could not go wrong, so he clasped his hands. “You are too kind!”

“Now tell me: when you say you must consider my interests, what do you mean?” “You're warm-hearted enough to volunteer for Xincheng, and Prefect Wang certainly wants your help. But he thinks as I do: you must not expose yourself to danger. Unless there's a completely safe plan, better not to go. If he raises the matter and you see difficulties, speak frankly.” Hu strengthened his tone. “Above all, don't take risks. That's what I mean by considering your interests.” “I'm deeply obliged.” Ji answered calmly. “There's no completely safe plan for such a business. Everything depends on thorough preparation and the ability to adapt when the moment comes. Rest assured, Brother Xueyan: I do have ways of protecting myself.”

“It's a pity Xincheng is in the mountains. If it were a river port, I could guarantee your safety.” “Why?” Ji asked. “Are you well acquainted with the naval forces?” “No.” After a moment's thought, Hu decided he might as well be candid. “I have friends in the Grain Transport Brotherhood.” “Excellent!” Ji became excited. “I've been wanting to meet some of them. You must introduce me.” He added, “I have no ulterior purpose. I'm simply interested in the way these men live. I'd like to compare them with the Biographies of Knight-Errants and see how the present differs from the past.” What were the Biographies of Knight-Errants? Hu had no idea. Twice in a few moments he had failed to understand Ji, and it troubled him. He really had read too few books. But what he did not know he could guess. Evidently Ji merely wished to make these acquaintances. Men of the brotherhood were expansive in their friendships; the more friends, the better. Neither Yu Si nor You Wu would think the introduction presumptuous. Hu agreed at once. “Brother Heling, I'm an outsider. But in the past year or so I've made two splendid friends on the waterways, one in Huzhou and one in Songjiang. When your official business is finished and I've returned from Shanghai, let's visit Huzhou together. Naturally we'll impose on Prefect Wang. I'll introduce you to a friend named Yu. With your temperament, you're certain to get on.”

“Excellent!” Ji gladly raised his cup. After draining it, he asked, “When do you leave for Shanghai?” “I should have left the day before yesterday. But I couldn't abandon Prefect Wang here alone, so I got off the boat after boarding it.” “Ah! That deserves another full cup!” Ji took the wine pot, filled his cup, drank it dry, and showed it to Hu. “Few men nowadays are so quick to help a friend in trouble or so generous in the old-fashioned way.” This Hu understood. His reply was immediate. “There is at least one other: your most distinguished self.” He returned the toast, which Ji happily accepted. Setting down his cup, Ji looked almost overcome with pleasure. “Brother Xueyan, meetings between people truly depend on what the Buddhists call yinyuan—causes and affinities. You cannot force them in the least.” “Oh, so yinyuan comes from Buddhist scripture?” Hu had taken the word to mean the ties that bring a marriage about.

Ji was surprised. Hu spoke so well; how could he not know the origin of yinyuan? Yet the passing trace of condescension vanished at once. When friends take to one another, charitable explanations readily follow. Though a merchant with little schooling, Hu was not vulgar. Through social intercourse he had acquired an elegant way of speaking that carried him creditably through formal occasions. That was no small achievement. Ji had not yet noticed that Hu understood a different word, also pronounced yinyuan: marriage ties rather than causes and affinities. He simply developed his thought. “People speak only of affinity, but there must be a cause before affinity can arise. Our temperaments are one such cause. You understood that I respond to kindness, not pressure, and that poverty hasn't destroyed my self-respect. That's why we get on. When people say they lack affinity, what they really lack is a cause for it. If their aspirations differ and their temperaments clash, how can they become friends?” Only then did Hu realise that Ji meant yin as in cause and effect, not yin as in marriage. He felt still more uncomfortable, but saw no need to conceal it. “Brother Heling,” he said sincerely, “when it comes to principles from books, I'm no match for you. But please go on. Listening can only do me good.”

This made Ji like him still more for his candour, though it also left him reluctant to continue displaying quotations and book learning. “To understand the world is learning; to comprehend human dealings is literature. Brother Xueyan, there's no need to be so modest. When you have leisure, try reading a few poems and looking at mountains and water. It would nourish your temperament and do you a great deal of good.” “Those words are a prescription,” Hu said with a smile. “They could cure my vulgarity.” “Exactly!” Ji tapped in appreciation. “A man who sees that is no vulgar fellow.” His pleasure in conversation increased, and with it his appetite for wine. They ordered another two jin of Zhuyeqing. The proprietor, too, knew how to oblige. From a bamboo basket suspended in the lake, he took a black carp weighing three jin. Instead of preparing it in the traditional vinegar style handed down from the Southern Song, he borrowed a Shanxi method and made a fish soup with vinegar and pepper, refreshing to the stomach and calculated to clear the effects of wine. He brought it himself, explaining that it was a complimentary dish. Ji's appetite improved as well. After three bowls of dongchun rice, he rubbed his stomach. “This is the first time since my wife died that I've eaten and drunk to such contentment.”

The remark reminded Hu of something. “Brother Heling, your wife left five or six children. Someone must manage the household. Surely you've considered marrying again?” “Ah!” Ji sighed. “Of course I have. But consider it: five or six children to look after, and a wretched expectant official who doesn't know what year he'll receive a post. What daughter of even a moderately respectable family would marry me?” “That's true,” Hu replied. “Let me think about it for you.” Ji merely smiled. Hu, however, really did think, and soon had an idea. He kept it to himself for the moment and turned to other small talk. The sun had sunk between the Northern and Southern Peaks, scattering ten thousand golden scales across the lake. The heat was less fierce than at noon, and a breeze beneath the willows cleared their heads. Truly, “The setting sun is beautiful beyond measure, but twilight is near.” Twilight meant the city gates would soon close. Reluctantly, they parted, agreeing to meet the next day.

Hu went straight to Wang's house. Wang was seeing a visitor out. As soon as he saw Hu, he caught his hand and laughed. “Xueyan, you're astonishing! To win over a man like that—I can only admire you. I've called on him and left eight taels as a condolence offering. That wasn't too little, was it?” “The amount doesn't matter,” Hu replied. “He's already volunteered. He'll certainly return your visit tomorrow morning, and you can speak to him directly.” “Volunteered?” All Wang's worries vanished. “Excellent! I'll give a dinner tomorrow evening and invite Brigade Commander Kui and the two gentlemen from Xincheng. We can discuss everything properly. Come early.” The next afternoon, Hu finished lunch at home and went to Wang's as arranged. Ji soon arrived too. He had returned Wang's call that morning and accepted the dinner invitation. They had also agreed that he should come early so they could devise a concrete plan. Once Kui and the Xincheng gentlemen arrived, they could settle it together and begin work immediately.

“Brother Heling,” Wang began, “I've been considering matters ever since your visit this morning. The rebel monk Huixin has murdered the Xincheng magistrate, and the county's deputy magistrate is now holding the seal. I mean to recommend you to the governor as acting magistrate. With the seal of authority in your hands, your work would be easier. Of course, this would only be temporary. Xincheng has poor soil and impoverished inhabitants. You shouldn't be kept in such an unrewarding post. Later I'll certainly help you transfer to a large county of the first class.” Ji clasped his hands. “Thank you for advancing my interests, Mr Xuexuan. But for now I should retain the title of commissioner. Why? First, I must adapt to circumstances. I may have to enter the tiger's den and temporarily call those rebels brothers, drinking with them on friendly terms. As their magistrate, I would have to preserve the dignity of the court. That would constrain me everywhere and make things harder. Second, the deputy magistrate is holding the seal and doing his best to sustain a city in danger. He must hope to gain something for his efforts. If I take the acting appointment, his hopes disappear. Even if he doesn't resent it and obstruct me at every turn, he'll certainly lose his enthusiasm. That would do our purpose no good.”

“Yes, yes!” Wang's admiration showed in both his words and expression. “Your analysis displays real insight. We'll do exactly as you advise. Once this affair is settled, leave your substantive appointment to me.” “That is for later. For now, please recommend to the authorities that if the deputy magistrate of Xincheng renders distinguished service, they should promote him to act as magistrate instead of sending someone else. ‘A generous reward will bring forth brave men’ is sometimes a very useful principle. With that promise from above, my work in Xincheng would become much easier.” “Quite right! And he deserves it. He's holding the place together in danger and should receive that recognition. It would be grossly unfair to leave him all the hardship, then let another man enjoy the fruits once order is restored.” They went on to discuss the details of attempting conciliation before resorting to force. Hu saw no part for himself and could contribute nothing, so he quietly withdrew and went straight to the inner rooms to see Mrs Wang.

Mrs Wang was warmer than ever, calling him “Brother” at every turn and treating him almost as a member of her own family. Hu understood official households: they might be familiar, but others must not overstep the forms. He therefore continued to address her properly. “Mrs Wang, you needn't worry about Mr Xuexuan any longer. Ji Heling admires him, and he and I felt like old friends at our first meeting. He's agreed to go to Xincheng.” “It's all your doing, Brother!” she said with difficulty. “Truly, I don't know how to thank you.” “There's no need. Even if I have been of some help, with my friendship for Mr Xuexuan it was only right. Mr Ji is the one we truly owe. To speak plainly, we must appreciate what he's doing by going there.” Hu continued, “Just now Mr Xuexuan offered to recommend him as acting magistrate, but he firmly refused, saying it would make the work harder. Think of it: an expectant official waits for nothing but a post. Why would he put aside rank and advancement when they're offered? Simply for friendship.”

“That's true,” Mrs Wang said. “Brother, we're among ourselves. Give me some advice. I can't inquire into official business or interfere with it, but personally he's doing your elder brother a great service. I must show some consideration too. If his wife were alive, it would be easier. We women could visit, and anything could be discussed. Unfortunately, she's dead.” This was the crucial point. Hu had guided the conversation here in a few sentences and was about to state his purpose when someone arrived. He swallowed the words already on his tongue. “Please have some tea, Mr Hu. It's flag-and-spear tea from Lion Hill, sent by Magistrate Chen of Qiantang. We've only just opened it. You're particular about tea—do try this fresh batch.” The speaker was Mrs Wang's trusted maid, Ruiyun. Tall and graceful, she had a long face and a rather broad chin. In physiognomy, however, a full, well-shaped lower face was supposed to promise distinction. Her bearing did indeed suggest a young woman from a good family. She spoke calmly, carried herself quietly, and showed no frivolity. Her particular gift was household management: she kept everything in perfect order and was virtually Mrs Wang's right arm. Thus, though well into marriageable adulthood, she remained unmarried, simply because her mistress could not bear to let her go.

“Thank you, thank you!” Hu smiled. “Ruiyun, how old are you?” She dreaded being asked her age; the subject hurt her. Yet she was no ordinary woman and answered with composure. “Twenty-two this year.” She was actually twenty-five and had subtracted three years. “You don't look twenty-two,” Hu said, deliberately trying to please her. “I thought you were under twenty.” Ruiyun smiled openly and charmingly. Her mouth was rather large, but her even white teeth kept the smile from being unattractive in the least. “Brother!” Mrs Wang sounded anxious. “Are you...” Hu coughed loudly to stop her. He knew what she was about to ask and thought it awkward to say before Ruiyun. How could Ruiyun fail to notice? Taking one of Mrs Wang's teacups, she unobtrusively withdrew. Only then did Mrs Wang ask quietly, “Brother, do you mean to find Ruiyun a husband?”

“I do have that thought, though I must first know your wishes,” Hu answered frankly. “I don't think it can be put off any longer.” Mrs Wang blushed. “I won't conceal it from you. First, the higher matches are beyond us and the lower ones won't do. Second, I really can't manage without her.” “That was true before. Things are different now.” “Yes, different.” She was merely agreeing politely; she did not really know how things had changed. Hu saw this. Trusting in the closeness of their friendship, he thought he must explain plainly, or the conversation would go no further. “Mrs Wang, a little over a year ago, before Mr Xuexuan went to the capital, I knew something of your circumstances. It was your management that carried the household through those hard times and allowed his fortune to turn. Naturally, then, you couldn't do without a capable helper like Ruiyun...” “Ah!” She interrupted before he could finish, her face full of uneasy remorse. “You're right, Brother! Thank you for reminding me.” He had made her see the difference between then and now. The masters were enjoying official success and rising rapidly; what of the servants? Ruiyun had helped them endure hardship and deserved some reward. How could Mrs Wang bear to neglect her future and let her youth slip away? She was now not merely uneasy but anxious to find, immediately if possible, a promising husband of suitable age and appearance for Ruiyun.

“Tell me, Brother, whose family is it? What is the man's background? How old is he? If the proposal seems suitable, I want to see him for myself.” Her eager concern showed that her expectations were high. Ji could not take Ruiyun as a formally married successor to his late wife, and he had six children still under age. Mention either fact, and Mrs Wang would shake her head at once. If Hu met a refusal at the outset, recovering the position would be difficult even if possible. His first words must move her and leave no room for rejection. That required a little manoeuvring. However much she cared for Ruiyun, she cared more for her husband. He could begin there. “Mrs Wang, this marriage concerns Mr Xuexuan closely too. If I arrange it, everything will go smoothly. If I fail, trouble may follow.”

As he had expected, her expression changed again. Concern was joined by vigilance. “Brother, if you're arranging it, there's no reason it shouldn't succeed. Whatever you do is sound.” It was an excellent answer. It made Hu feel the weight of responsibility and obliged him to consider Ruiyun's interests. Instead of replying immediately, he reviewed Ji's qualities once more. In that brief silence, Mrs Wang understood. “Is the man you mean Mr Ji?” she asked directly. “It is.” Hu had finished his deliberation. “Let me speak frankly. If Ruiyun hopes to marry an official, she'll have to accept some disadvantages for the first few years. As for Ji himself, you can imagine his qualities. His character and ability are first-rate. He's certain to succeed. If she marries him, she will have good days ahead.” Mrs Wang considered silently, then asked, “How old is he?” “Just over forty. He looks young—only in his thirties—and is full of energy.” “What about his temper?” “Talented men generally have a temper, but they don't vent it at home. A man who's a tiger in his house and a timid cat beside the stove outside it is the most hopeless kind.” “Indeed!” Mrs Wang smiled. “What sort of man can do nothing but beat his wife at home?” Then she added, “That reminds me: why did you say Ruiyun must accept disadvantages for a couple of years? I don't quite understand.”

“I mean she wouldn't have the status of principal wife when she first entered his household. After two or three years, he would naturally elevate her to that position.” Mrs Wang had to consider this, less for the present than for the future. “Brother, you're being frank. But if Mr Ji later marries someone else to replace his wife, wouldn't Ruiyun's hopes come to nothing?” “We can make the condition clear beforehand.” Hu tapped his chest. “If he fails to honour it, come to me, the matchmaker.” “A full bowl is easy to eat; a sweeping promise is hard to keep. I trust you in everything, but on this matter, frankly, I've seen more than you. Many matchmakers labour hard and earn only blame. Otherwise, why would people talk about pounding the matchmaker into paste? Naturally our two families would never behave like that towards each other. If it happened, Ruiyun would simply have to suffer.” “It depends on the man. Ji's word is his bond. He may refuse to promise, but once he agrees, he'll keep faith. In short, if Ruiyun is truly capable and virtuous, they will grow old together.”

“Very well, leave that aside,” Mrs Wang said. “Does Mr Ji have elderly parents?” “No parents above him, but six little devils below!” This was the greatest obstacle to the match, and Hu deliberately raised it himself. “Still, don't worry. The family is well brought up. All six children are very good.” She shook her head as he spoke. “That makes it difficult! What do you men know of the labour of running a household? With six children, making shoes alone would keep her busy all year. If she later has children of her own, wouldn't that add hardship to hardship?” From this point Hu spent a great many words. His eloquence was extraordinary and had usually carried everything before it. Now, however, nothing could persuade Mrs Wang. He praised Ruiyun's ability: she could make light work of the most complicated household. He said Ji would soon advance and could employ more servants to share the burden. Every argument failed before her single answer: “Ruiyun has suffered for years. I won't send her out to suffer again!” Further talk was useless. Hu gradually drew back. Though the affair had failed, goodwill remained intact. Mrs Wang, deeply apologetic, left an opening: “We can discuss it again later.”

Hu could not wait. A favour of this sort had to be carried through briskly if its recipient was to feel its full value. He therefore tried another route, through Wang. But if Wang simply overruled his wife, she would be unhappy and their marriage might suffer. Hu devised a gentler plan. “My dear,” Wang said in a consultative tone, “Ji Heling is doing our whole family a great service. We've just settled it over dinner: he'll leave for Xincheng the day after tomorrow. Since he's helping us, we must consider his difficulties too.” “Naturally. What difficulties does he have just now, and how can we help?” “He's acting as both father and mother. Once he leaves, the old family servant won't be able to manage everything. I'd like Ruiyun to keep house for him for a few days.” Mrs Wang smiled. “This must be one of Xueyan's devices.” “He's exceptionally clever. A device of his won't go wrong.”

“I'm not saying it's wrong,” she replied. “But you must explain the device before I can understand it.” “This is what he means. First, Ruiyun can manage Ji's household for a few days so he can leave without domestic worries. Second, she can see the situation for herself. If she finds him agreeable, the children obedient, and the household within her abilities, nothing could be better. Otherwise we abandon the idea and never mention it again, leaving no trace of the proposal. Wouldn't that be excellent?” “Yes, yes!” Mrs Wang nodded vigorously. “I have no objection to that.” “But let me offer some advice too,” Wang continued. “To be fair, a man like Ji has real talent. If he becomes a little more accommodating, his bearing and ability will certainly bring success. Ruiyun may have some hardship at first, but later she will enjoy prosperity. Besides, once we're close friends and this marriage links us too, you could visit each other often. Wouldn't that be pleasant?” This persuaded her. Affection required some consideration for herself as well as for Ruiyun. Whether Ruiyun became wife or concubine, relations between the women would depend first on relations between the men. Differences of rank or generation, or husbands who rarely met, made it difficult for their households' women to associate comfortably. Wang and Ji would certainly see much of each other. As friends whose families visited freely, they would give her ample opportunity to see Ruiyun. She therefore happily summoned the maid and explained the entire proposal, emphasising first that they could visit often, then promising a dowry, and finally asking what she thought.

Ruiyun had already been listening through the wall while Hu and Wang discussed the matter with their mistress. It concerned the rest of her life, and she had been considering it throughout. She felt it best not to declare herself yet. “Mr Ji is undertaking official business for the master. With no one to manage his household, naturally I should do it for a few days. Who can say what comes afterwards?” “That's reasonable too.” Mrs Wang wanted her to make a special effort and win Ji's heart, but could not say so openly. Instead she challenged her pride. “Only I'm a little worried. He has so many children, and the household will be hard to manage. It would sound very bad if people later said, ‘Her being there made no difference.’” Ruiyun said nothing, but inwardly scoffed. No difference? She would show them what proper management looked like tomorrow. Then they would know.

Early the next morning, Ruiyun took a clothes chest and travelled in a small sedan chair to Ji's house, accompanied by Gao Sheng. Hu had already explained the arrangement to Ji, who was deeply grateful. He treated Ruiyun with special respect, calling her “Miss Rui” and telling his children to address her as “Aunt Rui.” “Miss Rui, I'm putting you to a great deal of trouble,” he said earnestly. “With your help I can set my mind at rest. From today, I entrust this household to you. If the children misbehave, scold or punish them as necessary. Don't hesitate.” “How could I do such a thing?” she answered with a faint smile, drawing his youngest, large-eyed daughter into her arms while surveying the five older children. There were exactly three boys and three girls. The eldest, a boy, looked thoroughly honest and good-natured. The second was a thin girl of about twelve, with unusually lively eyes and more to say than anyone else. She was plainly not easy to manage. To run this household well, Ruiyun thought, she must first win over this Second Miss. “Miss Rui!” Ji interrupted her thoughts. “Let me give you the keys.” A housekeeper's keys were like an official's seal. Ruiyun accepted the heavy bunch without hesitation. Ji then summoned Zhang Gui and a young maid named Xiaoqing and introduced them. Having explained these arrangements, he rose to go out.

“Mr Ji, will you be home for a meal?” Ruiyun asked. “I leave tomorrow, and there's much to arrange today. I can't get back for lunch, and I have a dinner engagement.” “Then your luggage needs packing?” “I must trouble you with that. I won't take much. I usually bring Zhang Gui when I travel, but this time he needn't come. He knows what I require.” Ji did not return until the second watch that evening, bringing a guest: Hu Xueyan. The moment he entered, he felt the difference. The passage was no longer so dark that he could scarcely see. Pale moonlight made it quite bright. Looking closely, he saw that the windows had been repapered. Inside, everything stood in order. All the miscellaneous objects that had cluttered the reception room had been removed. The fresh clarity of the house immediately recalled the days when his wife was alive.

“Mr Ji is home!” Ruiyun came from the inner rooms to greet him, then welcomed Hu. “You've taken such trouble!” Ji smiled broadly and clasped his hands in thanks. “Well?” Hu asked with satisfaction. “Didn't I say Miss Rui was capable?” “More than capable. She has both ability and virtue.” This was plainly the language of assessing a bride. Otherwise, why speak of “ability and virtue” in a guest temporarily managing the house? Ruiyun understood, but felt she must pretend not to. Calmly she directed Xiaoqing to pour tea and prepare the water pipe. Only when host and guest were seated did she say that she had cooked some fragrant rice congee, ready to serve whenever they felt hungry. Before Ji could answer, Hu welcomed the suggestion. “Just what I was wanting!” Ruiyun went out and returned with a tray: four small dishes, a pot of Ji's usual rose spirit, and an earthenware pot of hot congee. Whatever the food might taste like, the utensils were exceptionally clean and fine. Since his wife's death, Ji had made do with the barest arrangements. To see even a simple supper presented properly naturally pleased him.

“Come, come!” he urged his guest. “This truly is offering the Buddha someone else's flowers. Without Miss Rui, I'd have nothing fit to serve you.” “Mr Ji!” Ruiyun was pleased too, though she thought his repeated courtesies unnecessary. “You'll embarrass me. Since I've come here, these things are simply my duty. I only hope you'll forgive anything I fail to do properly.” She gave him a deep look before lowering her head to ladle the congee. From their manner, Hu knew the match would succeed and could not resist a joke. “Brother Heling, you really do treat each other with the respect due to honoured guests!” “She is a guest,” Ji replied. “Of course I should respect her.” The phrase also described the mutual courtesy of an exemplary married couple. Ruiyun understood Hu's meaning but could think of no suitable answer. Still pretending not to understand, she quietly withdrew.

Watching her disappear, Hu moved from the seat opposite Ji to one beside him, across the corner of the table. He lowered his voice. “Brother Heling, now for serious business. What do you think?” Pressed so directly, Ji felt embarrassed. He smiled and tried to postpone the matter. “There'll be time to discuss it when I return from Xincheng.” “Certainly. Ordinarily that would be right. But the moment you leave, I must hurry to Shanghai. We're close friends now, so I'll be frank: everything I own is tied up in those boatloads of silk. I'm afraid of trouble on the journey. That's too complicated to explain now, so let it pass. Once in Shanghai, I must wait for an opportunity to sell. It may be two or three months before I return. You'll be back in Hangzhou long before then. Suppose you two are fond of each other and have to wait for the matchmaker. You'd be anxious, and so would I. Better to arrange the match now, before I leave. Whether I make it back for the wedding feast doesn't matter.” “You are kindness itself!” Ji offered him a toast, using the pause to consider. He still felt they should not hurry. “Could you give me a little longer to observe?” he asked apologetically.

“What more is there to observe?” Hu objected. “First, with your judgement and mine, can't we see what sort of person she is? Second, unless she possessed the ability and virtue you praised, would Mrs Wang have treasured her so much that she kept her unmarried until this age?” “That's true.” “And frankly, taking a concubine isn't the same as marrying a principal wife. There's no need for so much deliberation.” “Very well. I'll obey.” Ji offered another toast, thanking him as matchmaker. “Not so fast! You promise to obey, but I haven't given my instructions yet. I've pledged my word to Mrs Wang: if after two or three years Ruiyun has given no cause for complaint, you must be ready to obtain an imperial patent of rank for her.” “Naturally. I shan't marry another principal wife. In due course I'll raise her to that position.” “Those are your own words.” Hu deliberately pressed the point. “Will you turn into a Cai Bojie or a Chen Shimei and abandon her later? We must settle this beforehand, so I can answer for it.” Ji laughed. “What an idea! I'm not going to become the top examination graduate. Where would a prime minister's offer of his daughter's hand come from?”

“I don't believe you're that sort of man either. Then my work as matchmaker is done. You can choose the auspicious day yourselves. Mrs Wang will provide a dowry as though marrying off a daughter. As for your betrothal gift, there are two ways. Choose one.” “That's a new idea. Tell me the amount, and I'll find it. What is there to choose?” “I always do things differently. First, given the friendship among all three parties, I think the gift could be waived. Second, if you insist on doing your future companion proper honour, I'll lend you the money. Choose for yourself.” “Naturally I must do her honour. Besides, I already owe Mrs Wang a great deal. The betrothal gift cannot be omitted.” Ji reflected. “Borrowing is easy; repayment is difficult.” “Not difficult at all. Once you complete the Xincheng assignment, Governor Huang is certain to give you a post—perhaps a county under Mr Xuexuan's Huzhou prefecture. Would you still fear being unable to repay?” Ji considered the matter as a whole and decided the loan was reasonable. He nodded. “I'll borrow a thousand taels from your bank. But charge the usual interest, or I won't take it.”

Without a word, Hu took a sheaf of banknotes from an inner pocket of his jacket, selected one, and laid it before Ji. It was for exactly a thousand taels. “You certainly act promptly!” Ji laughed. “And you certainly cultivate your customers!” “I run a bank. How could I do otherwise? Put the note away safely. If you'd like to open an account at Fukang, ask for my chief clerk, Liu Qingsheng.” “Thank you. First let me write a promissory note.” Hu was prepared for this too. He carried a leather writing wallet containing blank plum-red paper ruled in eight columns, an inkbox, and a brush. In his calligraphy after Su Shi, dignified yet graceful, Ji wrote out the note on the spot and handed it back together with the banknote. “Why this?” Hu asked in surprise, pointing to the money. “The betrothal gift! I leave early tomorrow, so I must trouble you, my distinguished matchmaker, to prepare the formal card and deliver it for me.” “There's no need for so much...” “No, no!” Ji interrupted. “Even ten measures of pearls would seem a meagre gift to me.”

Hu considered. “Very well. Now tell me, when do you intend to hold the wedding?” “Since it's settled, naturally the sooner the better. Otherwise I fear Ruiyun will be left in an awkward position.” Ji continued, “If, as you say, I return successfully from Xincheng and receive a magistrate's seal, won't she be an official's lady?” “If that's your thinking, I must advise you...” Hu, too, produced a literary phrase. “Have patience; do not be hasty.” “Quite right. I'll follow your advice.” Ji agreed gladly. “Besides, we must wait for you to return. I'll have her thank the matchmaker at the feast!”

At first the two men had discussed Ruiyun in lowered voices, with some restraint. As they went on, they spoke louder and louder. Ruiyun could not have avoided hearing even if she had wished. Sitting quietly behind the door, she felt her heart tighten again and again until she almost struggled for breath. The words “an official's lady” were particularly sweet, like a piece of sugar in her mouth. Yet something continued to trouble her. Surely they ought at least to sound out her wishes first! They seemed so certain of her, so confident of their hold, that they were already deciding the wedding date between themselves. And “thank the matchmaker”! How did they know she would not object? Did they suppose she would accept whatever they said and let herself be arranged as they pleased? While she was thinking this, Ji called, “Miss Rui!” “Coming!” Her hand reached the curtain, then withdrew. She touched her face. It was indeed warm. She could hardly appear like this. Yet failing to come would reveal that she had been listening. After a moment she lifted the curtain and went out, but stood some distance away with her hands at her sides.

“Ruiyun,” Hu said, “I'm leaving.” “I'll light the lantern.” She welcomed the excuse to withdraw again. “No hurry. I have something to ask you.” “Yes, Mr Hu?” “Mr Ji is deeply grateful for your management of his household. He's asked me to buy you something in Shanghai. Don't be shy. Tell me what you'd like.” “I couldn't accept such kindness,” she replied. “How could I let Mr Ji spend money on me?” “Don't stand on ceremony. Tell me yourself. If you don't,” Hu added, “I'll buy a whole heap of things and charge them to your Mr Ji. That would cost him far more!”

What a formidable man this Mr Hu was, Ruiyun thought. She could not tell whether he was serious. If he really brought back a pile of useless things, she would regret the waste even though it was not her own money. Apparently it would be better to state her wishes. Yet Ruiyun also knew how to speak. “You're Mr Ji's good friend. You wouldn't let him spend too much.” She glanced at Ji and added, “I'll leave it to your judgement.” “That's an answer too. With your permission, I can act. In short, I'll satisfy you both: one won't feel it in the heart, and the other won't feel it in the purse.” There was a hidden judgement beneath the teasing. Ji frowned and Ruiyun blushed. Unwilling to remain there, she curtsied. “Thank you, Mr Hu and Mr Ji.” Then she turned away. “Well?” Hu said triumphantly. “She's protecting your interests at every turn. She's hardly entered the house and is already a devoted helpmate!” Ji pressed two fingers to his lips for silence, pointed towards the inner rooms, and asked softly, “Why embarrass her?” Hu laughed again. “Good! She protects you, and you protect her. It seems this match really will earn me merit for doing good.” Still talking, he moved towards the door. Ruiyun had roused the drowsing Zhang Gui and lit the lantern. Master and servant accompanied Hu outside, returning only after he had entered his chair.

Ji checked his luggage, then instructed Zhang Gui to obey Miss Rui in everything and guard the house carefully. When the servant had withdrawn, he asked, “Which room are you using, Miss Rui?” “I'm sharing with the Second Miss...” “Miss Rui,” Ji interrupted, “she's only a child. She doesn't deserve such a formal title from you. Call her by her name. It's Danhe...” He told her the names of all six children. “I wouldn't presume to call them simply by name either,” Ruiyun answered calmly. “I'll use guan.” In Jiangnan gentry households, children were commonly addressed with guan, attached either to their place in the family or to part of their name. Danhe would thus become Heguan. It was a customary form that implied neither superiority nor inferiority, so Ji offered no further polite objection.

“Let me say again, Miss Rui: I entrust the entire household to you, and all the children to your care.” “Set your mind at rest, Mr Ji. I'll attend to everything here.” Ruiyun now felt differently about him. A vague sense that he might become her lifelong support made her concerned for his safety on this journey. Yet she could not say so plainly and merely asked, “When do you expect to return?” “It shouldn't take long. A fortnight if things go quickly, a month at most. I'm confident I can settle the business.” “I hear it's a very troublesome affair?” “Much depends on the man.” Afraid she might not understand the saying, Ji explained, “It depends on who handles it. If I go, I should be able to manage.” “And if you can't?” If he failed, his life would be at stake. But he understood her feelings and would not frighten her with the truth. “Don't worry,” he said with complete confidence. “I shall certainly manage it.”

Ruiyun's face did indeed relax. She had many more questions, but it was their first day together, and the limits of her position made them hard to ask. Yet she could not bear to leave. She stood with her head lowered, as though waiting for further instructions. Ji found the atmosphere stiff and unsuitable for deeper conversation. “Please sit down. We shall have many more days together. If we're so constrained, we won't feel like one family.” The words were quite explicit. Sitting as he asked would amount to acknowledging that they were one family. Though she cared greatly about him, she did not want to show openly that she had given him her heart and her future. She was shy; besides, a trace of inexplicable resentment towards him and Hu remained, prompting deliberate reserve. Seeing her still standing, Ji quickly repeated, “Do sit down.” “I'm quite all right.” She still would not comply. Without realising it, Ji rose too. Holding his water pipe and twisting paper spills, he talked with her, chiefly asking about her family background. She answered every question. They continued until the third watch before finally going to their separate rooms.

This should have been Ji's most comfortable night since his bereavement. Ruiyun had thoroughly put his bed in order: spotless white ramie curtains, a scrupulously wiped sleeping mat, and a fresh pillow cover. The shelf behind the large bed was neatly arranged, with tea and books ready. Outside the curtains, the oil lamp had been trimmed to burn brightly, so he could read if unable to sleep. He could not sleep, but he did not read. His eyes were already dry and tired, while his mind remained excited and crowded with thoughts. Above all, he was assessing the journey to Xincheng. At first, moved by Hu's friendship and Wang's courtesy, he had volunteered without counting the consequences. Now he saw that he could not simply act on courage and consider the rest afterwards. What to do on arrival would necessarily depend on circumstances, but success and failure both required forethought. No one entering a city in danger could devise an entirely safe plan. If he were killed, what would become of his six children? Naturally there would be an allowance from the court and help from his superiors. But these depended on others' generosity. He needed someone truly dependable to whom he could entrust the children if they were orphaned.

This naturally brought Hu to mind. Ji regretted not having considered it sooner. Had he done so, he could have made a serious, explicit request that evening. Now he could only leave something like a will. He rose again, moved the lamp to the table, and laid out paper and brush, but hesitated. A will seemed too grave. It would place a heavy burden on Hu. He considered for a long while, then suddenly found an ingenious solution that pleased him greatly.
